hook.text: Interval training is sold on fat loss.
Pool the trials, rate how far each result can be trusted, and the order flips.

populationPanel.text: Who was studied: 1,130 adults with a mean age of 26.27 years, across thirty-six randomized trials lasting 3 to 15 weeks.
Most were inactive and overweight or obese, so the findings describe that group best.
Children, teenagers and people with a known disease were left out.

paragraphs.text: Compared with no exercise, interval training in these adults reduced fat mass by 1.86 kg and body fat percentage by 1.53 points.
Fat-free mass, the weight of everything in the body that is not fat, went up by 0.51 kg.
Then the authors rated how far each result can be trusted, using a system called GRADE.
Fat-free mass: high.
Fat mass: moderate.
Body fat percentage: low.
The body-fat trials disagreed with one another heavily; the fat-free-mass trials did not.

sections.heading: How sure is the lean-mass number?

paragraphs.text: The 95% confidence interval for fat-free mass runs from 0.06 kg to 0.95 kg.
At its weak end that is 0.06 kg, an amount no bathroom scale would register.
High certainty here means the trials agree that the average effect is above zero.
It does not mean the effect is big.
Take one trial out of the pool and the lean-mass effect is gone: the estimate becomes 0.46 kg lost, with an interval from 1.38 kg lost to 0.44 kg gained.
So the result graded most certain also rests on a single study.
The second surprise is which kind of training did what.
Only cycling raised fat-free mass in these trials, by 0.63 kg (95% CI 0.17 to 1.09).
Running did not.
Overground running showed the widest drop in body fat percentage, 2.80 points (95% CI 3.89 to 1.71), but that is the low-certainty outcome.
Treadmill running did not clearly change fat mass at all: its interval runs from 2.82 kg lost to 0.62 kg gained.
Across outcomes the same settings kept landing on the favourable side: more than 8 weeks, three sessions a week, work bursts under 60 seconds, rests of 90 seconds or less, and moving during the rest.
These come from comparing subgroups of trials, not from testing one setting directly against another, so treat them as leads.
The authors note an earlier pooled analysis that found no clear effect of cycling on fat mass in overweight and obese adults.
They also raise a practical point: heavier bodies load the joints differently when running, which is one reason cycling may suit some people whatever the averages say.

limitations.text: Most trials enrolled inactive adults who were overweight or obese.
The results may not carry over to people who already train.
The trials disagreed with each other, most of all on body fat percentage, which is why that result is graded low.
Body composition was measured with different tools from trial to trial, from skinfold calipers to DEXA scans.
The fat-free-mass result disappears when a single trial is removed.

daytime-caffeine-sleep.text: The schedule tested was three doses, the last one 475 minutes after waking, which came 8 hours before bed.
The finding covers a steady daily habit.
The authors caution that it may not hold after several days without caffeine.
Bedtime at home drifted about 25 minutes later on caffeine, so watch the clock as well as the cup.

hiit-body-composition.text: If lean mass is the aim, the supported combination in these trials was cycling intervals, three sessions a week, for more than 8 weeks.
Keep work bursts to 60 seconds or less: longer bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass, with an interval from 2.28 kg lost to 0.57 kg gained.
Standing still between bursts showed no clear gain in fat-free mass.
Two sessions a week did not clearly change body fat percentage; three did.

steps-days-per-week.text: If a daily target keeps failing, the study's lowest active group is a reasonable place to start: 8,000 steps on 1 to 2 days a week.
Past 3 to 4 such days the association flattened, so a missed day is no reason to write off the week.
The association was widest in adults aged 65 and over, at 19.9 points against 7.4 points in younger adults.

turmeric-pepper-breakfast.text: The dose tested was 1 g of black pepper, cooked into the egg of a toast-and-tea breakfast.
The glucose difference showed 30 minutes after eating and not in the 3-hour total.
Turmeric alone, at 1 g, showed no clear difference in glucose.
